neurological_exam.mental_status: GCS 13 (E3V4M6). Disoriented to time. Slowed speech. Asterixis mild bilaterally. Wife reports behavioral changes and mood swings for several months.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Kayser-Fleischer rings visible on slit-lamp examination — golden-brown deposits at corneal periphery. Pupils reactive. Extraocular movements intact with mild slowing of saccades. Mild dysarthria.
neurological_exam.motor: Wing-beating tremor bilateral arms. Increased tone (extrapyramidal). No focal weakness.
neurological_exam.coordination: Cerebellar-type dysmetria on finger-nose testing. Truncal ataxia.
neurological_exam.gait: Dystonic gait — unsteady with abnormal posturing.
neurological_exam.additional: No jaundice. Mild ascites. Wing-beating tremor, dystonia, and KF rings are NOT typical HE — they suggest Wilson's disease as underlying etiology.

patient.chief_complaint: Acute confusion, tremor, and dystonia in patient with cryptogenic cirrhosis
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. N. is a 55-year-old man with a 5-year history of 'cryptogenic cirrhosis' and tremor attributed to essential tremor, now presenting with acute worsening of confusion, tremor, and dystonia over 2 weeks. His wife reports he has had mood swings, behavioral changes, and difficulty with word-finding for several months — dismissed as depression and stress. His neurological exam reveals Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit-lamp, wing-beating tremor, cerebellar ataxia, and dystonia — findings not attributable to HE alone. The puzzle: (1) HE is present and contributing to confusion (ammonia moderately elevated), but (2) the underlying etiology of cirrhosis is likely Wilson's disease (not cryptogenic), (3) Wilson's disease has neuropsychiatric presentation distinct from HE, and (4) the acute HE episode may be precipitating on a background of Wilson's hepatolenticular degeneration. Copper metabolism tests are the key diagnostic missing piece. The agent must identify Wilson's disease as the underlying etiology, initiate chelation therapy, AND treat the acute HE.

output.proposed: Wilson's disease chelation therapy — trientine vs penicillamine, zinc acetate
interactions: Trientine 750-1000 mg TID (chelation) — preferred for neurological Wilson's (penicillamine can paradoxically worsen neurology by mobilizing copper acutely)
Penicillamine: effective chelator but avoided as first-line for neurological presentation due to copper mobilization worsening
Zinc acetate 50 mg elemental zinc TID — reduces intestinal copper absorption; used for maintenance
contraindications: Penicillamine as first-line for neurological Wilson's — paradoxical neurological worsening
Sertraline in Wilson's disease: unclear safety but continue unless clearly contributing; watch LFTs
warnings: Monitor CBC monthly — trientine can cause sideroblastic anemia
Diet: avoid high-copper foods (shellfish, liver, nuts, chocolate)
alternatives: Trientine 750 mg TID as initial chelation
Zinc acetate 50 mg TID after trientine stabilization
Liver transplant evaluation: if fulminant Wilson's disease with INR > 2 and rapidly worsening

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Hepatic encephalopathy (acute) superimposed on Wilson's disease neurological presentation (KF rings, wing-beating tremor, cerebellar ataxia, basal ganglia degeneration) — 'cryptogenic cirrhosis' diagnosis was unrecognized Wilson's disease

differential.key_features: Prior diagnosis of 'essential tremor' was wrong — wing-beating tremor + KF rings + low ceruloplasmin + elevated urine copper = Wilson's disease; essential tremor does not cause KF rings or cerebellar ataxia

differential.diagnosis: Alcoholic cirrhosis with acquired hepatocerebral degeneration
differential.key_features: Patient never drank alcohol; acquired hepatocerebral degeneration does not cause KF rings; ceruloplasmin low, urine copper elevated — specific to Wilson's
Wilson's neurological presentation IS present — but ammonia 78 confirms concurrent HE which requires HE-specific treatment alongside chelation

differential.diagnosis: Autoimmune hepatitis with neurological paraneoplastic syndrome
differential.key_features: Ceruloplasmin 8 and urine copper 284 are diagnostic for Wilson's; ANA/ASMA negative (tested separately); basal ganglia MRI changes are copper deposition not paraneoplastic

optimal_actions.expected_finding: HE resolves; Wilson's neurological symptoms improve over months

critical_actions: KF rings on slit-lamp are pathognomonic for Wilson's disease in liver disease patients — EVERY patient with unexplained cirrhosis should have slit-lamp exam
Low ALP in liver disease is a classic Wilson's disease clue — alkaline phosphatase is characteristically low or normal in Wilson's despite significant hepatic dysfunction
Trientine preferred over penicillamine for neurological Wilson's — penicillamine can paradoxically worsen neurological symptoms by acutely mobilizing copper
Wilson's disease is CURABLE with liver transplant — treat HE and chelate copper; refer for transplant evaluation if MELD rises
contraindicated_actions: Penicillamine as first-line for neurological Wilson's disease — use trientine
Dismissing tremor as essential tremor without slit-lamp exam in young cirrhotic patient
Continuing without copper metabolism testing in cryptogenic cirrhosis
key_reasoning_points: Wilson's disease is a treatable cause of cirrhosis — 'cryptogenic cirrhosis' in a patient <60 requires copper metabolism testing (ceruloplasmin, 24h urine copper, slit-lamp)
Three classic Wilson's disease clues: (1) KF rings, (2) low ceruloplasmin, (3) low ALP in liver disease — any two of three strongly suggest Wilson's
HE is concurrent with Wilson's neurological presentation but distinct — HE is treated with lactulose/rifaximin; Wilson's neurological symptoms require copper chelation
Family screening is mandatory after Wilson's diagnosis — siblings and children have 1 in 4 risk (autosomal recessive)

red_herrings.intended_effect: Accept prior essential tremor diagnosis; attribute all tremor to ET; focus only on HE management; miss Wilson's disease
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Wing-beating (postural, held position) tremor in a cirrhotic patient is NOT essential tremor — it is Wilson's disease until proven otherwise; essential tremor does not occur with cerebellar ataxia, KF rings, or basal ganglia CT changes

red_herrings.data_point: Low ALP 38 U/L in liver disease
red_herrings.intended_effect: Assume lab error or attribute to medication effect; miss this critical diagnostic clue for Wilson's disease
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: LOW alkaline phosphatase in liver disease is a RED FLAG — ALP is normally elevated in liver disease; paradoxically low ALP is a classic feature of Wilson's disease and acute fulminant hepatitis; should immediately trigger copper metabolism testing

metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: HE superimposed on unrecognized Wilson's disease masquerading as cryptogenic cirrhosis + essential tremor; KF rings, LOW ALP, wing-beating tremor, and bilateral basal ganglia CT changes are the diagnostic clues; trientine (not penicillamine) for neurological Wilson's
